opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that's one of the most exciting directions for us. Our models are trained on a broad base of public structural and sequence data, which gives them a strong general understanding of how molecules interact. But every partner, whether it's a big pharma company or a smaller biotech, sits on proprietary data that we'll never see in the public domain: years of assay results, binding measurements, failed campaigns, structures they've solved in-house for targets they care about.

The opportunity is to take that general foundation and adapt it to a partner's specific chemistry, targets, and modalities. In practice that can mean fine-tuning on their internal data, or setting up a tighter loop where the model proposes designs, they test them in the lab, and those results flow back in to sharpen the model for their program. Even a fairly modest amount of high-quality, well-labeled data on a target family can meaningfully shift performance where it matters to them.

A couple of things make this work. First, trust and data governance: partners need confidence that their data improves *their* model and isn't leaking into anyone else's. So we think carefully about isolation and deployment. Second, the data has to be the right kind. Negative results are incredibly valuable, and most organizations underappreciate how much signal is in the experiments that didn't work.

Longer term, I think the picture is a strong shared base model with a layer of partner-specific specialization on top. The base keeps getting better as the field advances, and each partner gets something increasingly tuned to the biology they're actually trying to drug. That combination is where I think you get real step changes in how quickly people can go from a target to a viable molecule.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we think about a lot, and I'd frame it as kind of the natural next step after what we've been doing with the base models. The foundation models we've trained on public structural data, PDB, and so on, are really good at the general physics of how molecules interact. But the thing is, every pharma partner we talk to is sitting on this enormous proprietary dataset that never makes it into the public domain. Binding assays, ADME data, selectivity panels, sometimes decades of work on a particular target class. And that data is often exactly the signal you need to go from "this looks plausible" to "this is actually going to work in a program."

So the way we think about tailoring is less "we build a bespoke model for each partner from scratch," and more that the base model becomes a prior, and then you fine-tune or condition on the partner's data to specialize it. The analogy I'd use is what happened with language models. You have a general model, and then you adapt it to a domain or a company's internal data, and the adapted model is dramatically more useful for that specific context even though the core capability came from pretraining.

There are a few things that make this hard, though, and I don't want to oversell it. One is that biological data is messy in ways that text isn't. Assays have batch effects, different labs measure things differently, and a lot of historical data was generated under conditions that aren't well documented. So a big part of the work is actually data engineering and figuring out what's trustworthy before you ever get to training. The second is that partners are, understandably, extremely protective of this data. So the architecture of how you do the fine-tuning matters a lot. We've spent a lot of time thinking about setups where the model can learn from the data without the data ever leaving the partner's environment, or where what comes back to us is weights rather than raw examples.

And then the third thing, which I think is actually the most interesting scientifically, is that when you do this across multiple partners, you start to see where the base model is systematically wrong, and that feeds back into how we build the next generation. So it's not just a one-way service. It becomes a flywheel where the specialized models tell us what the general model is missing.

Where I think this ends up is that in a few years, the question won't be "which model is best," it'll be "which model has learned the most from the data that matters for my problem." And that's a very different competitive landscape than just chasing benchmark numbers.

r001.rationale: The response describes adapting a general model to a company’s internal data, compares this to language-model specialization, and applies that approach to partners’ proprietary biological data.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a lot of potential there. A partner may have biological data that captures something very specific about the targets or therapeutic programs they care about. The opportunity is to take a model with broad capabilities and use that data to make it more useful for those particular problems.

The key question is whether that tailoring translates into better experimental outcomes. Can you propose better candidates, test them, and then use those results to improve the next round? That feedback loop is where I think this could become especially valuable.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a really interesting opportunity there. A partner may have proprietary data around a particular target or class of molecules that captures things we don’t see in public datasets. The question is how we combine that with a broadly capable model so it becomes more useful for the specific problems they care about.

And that could mean fine-tuning, but it could also mean changing how we condition the model or incorporate experimental feedback. You can imagine a loop where the model proposes candidates, the partner tests them, and those results inform the next round. The important thing is to show that the tailoring improves prospective experimental outcomes, rather than just making the model better at reproducing the data it’s already seen.
